title: Percent Change
coreInsight: Percent change measures change relative to a specific base, and that base can change from one step to the next.
targetLearnerRealization: A percent change is measured from a particular base, so successive changes usually act on different wholes.
learningObjectives: Identify the reference whole for a percent change.
Recover an original amount from a known final percentage.
Distinguish percentage-point change from relative percent change.

continuity.openingCallback: Use proportional scaling to make a percent act on a stated base, then replace that base with the changed amount.
closingSeeds: Repeated multiplicative changes can be tracked by their scale factors.
A reported percent is incomplete unless its reference amount is known.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Reverse percentage problems can use the final amount as the original base.
Percentage points and percent change are the same thing.
A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease returns to the start.

beats.purpose: Establish percent change as proportional scaling from a visible 100-unit base.
beats.expectedRealization: A 20% increase adds 20 units when the base is 100.
beats.transitionIn: A percent is a ratio to 100, and ratios scale with their quantities. Start with a base where that scaling is visible.
beats.prompt: A collection has 100 tiles and grows by 20%. How many tiles does it have now?

visual.ariaLabel: A complete bar representing one hundred tiles in ten groups of ten

response.feedback: Twenty percent of 100 is 20; add the change to the original amount.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The 20-tile increase makes a new total of 120 tiles.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find 20% of the original 100 tiles, then add that amount.

resolution.takeaway: A percent change acts on a specified starting amount.

beats.purpose: Make the changed amount become the reference whole for a second percent change.
beats.expectedRealization: Twenty percent of the new 120-tile base is 24, not 20.
beats.transitionIn: The collection is now 120 tiles. Freeze that changed collection and call all of it the new whole.
beats.prompt: The 120-tile collection now shrinks by 20%. How many tiles are removed?

options.text: 20 tiles, because the first change was 20 tiles.
24 tiles, because 20% is now taken from 120.
40 tiles, because the percents add.
120 tiles, because the whole is removed.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. The second 20% uses 120 as its base, so it removes 24 tiles.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask “20% of what?” The current whole contains 120 tiles.

steps.title: Finish the change
steps.body: 120 − 24 = 96, not 100. Equal percent changes do not undo each other because they act on different bases.

resolution.takeaway: After a change, the changed amount becomes the next reference whole.

beats.purpose: Name percent change and its reference base after the learner has experienced the base moving.
beats.expectedRealization: Percent change is a multiplicative comparison between a change and its current base.
beats.transitionIn: The same 20% removed different amounts because its whole changed.
beats.name: Percent change and reference base
beats.conciseDefinition: Percent change compares the amount of change with the value before that change. Each successive change uses the current value as its base.
beats.formalization: new amount = old amount × (1 + change rate), with a negative rate for a decrease

beats.purpose: Confront the additive-discount prediction in an authentic problem and replace it with changing-base reasoning.
beats.expectedRealization: The second discount is 20% of the reduced 70% price, so the total discount is 44%, not 50%.
beats.transitionIn: An increase made the base larger. Two discounts make it smaller twice; predict carefully before combining 30% and 20%.
beats.whyNow: The changing-base idea is established, so the authentic successive-discount trap can expose why adding the two rates fails.
beats.entryBridge: Use a $100 starting tag and relabel the amount left after the first discount as the new whole.
beats.exitBridge: The final $56 price means $44 of the original $100 was removed.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A 100-unit bar that changes which remaining amount counts as the current whole.
learnerPrompts: At the first step, find the 70 dollars remaining after 30% off.
When the second discount appears, identify its base and explain why 20% of 70 is 14, not 20.
At the final regrouping, compare the 44 removed cells with the original 100.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The discounts remove $30 and then $14, for $44 off the original $100.
beats.incorrectFeedback: After the first discount, take 20% of the $70 sale price—not 20% of the original $100.

steps.title: Compare with the original
steps.body: $100 − $56 = $44, so the total discount is 44%. The answer is B.

resolution.takeaway: Successive percentage changes multiply their remaining factors.

beats.purpose: Generalize successive changes as multiplication and revisit increase-then-decrease.
beats.expectedRealization: Multipliers compose; signed percentages do not simply add.
beats.transitionIn: The price kept 70%, then kept 80%. Record those two actions as scale factors.
beats.prompt: Which expression correctly represents a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease on an amount x?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The second multiplier acts on the already increased amount, and 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Translate each change into the fraction retained or created, then apply the factors in sequence.

steps.title: Translate each action
steps.body: A 20% increase keeps 120%, or multiplies by 1.20. A 20% decrease keeps 80%, or multiplies by 0.80.

steps.title: Compose
steps.body: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, so the result is 96% of the start—a net 4% decrease.

resolution.takeaway: Compose changes by multiplying their scale factors.

beats.purpose: Repair reverse-percent reasoning by distinguishing the final amount from the original base.
beats.expectedRealization: Undoing a percent change requires division by the retained multiplier.
beats.transitionIn: Forward changes multiply the old amount. Reverse the arrow by undoing that multiplication.
beats.prompt: After a 20% discount, a jacket costs $80. What was its original price?

options.text: $64, because 20% of 80 is 16.
$96, by adding 20% of 80.
$100, because 80 is 80% of the original.
$160, by doubling the sale price.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The $80 final price is 80% of the original, so divide by 0.80.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The final $80 is not the original base. It equals 80% of that unknown base.

steps.title: Write the retained part
steps.body: A 20% discount leaves 80% of the original price.

resolution.takeaway: Reverse a percent change by dividing by its multiplier.

beats.purpose: Distinguish an absolute difference in percentage rates from relative percent change.
beats.expectedRealization: A rise from 40% to 50% is 10 percentage points but a 25% relative increase.
beats.transitionIn: Percentages themselves can change. Their subtraction and their relative growth answer different questions.
beats.prompt: A success rate rises from 40% to 50%. Which description is correct?

options.text: It rises 10 percentage points and 25% relative to the old rate.
It rises 10 percentage points and 10% relative to the old rate.
It rises 25 percentage points and 10% relative to the old rate.
It does not change because both values are percents.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. The rate gains 10 points; that gain is one quarter of the original 40%.
beats.incorrectFeedback: First subtract the displayed rates. Then compare that 10-point increase with the original 40%.

steps.title: Relative percent change
steps.body: The increase is 10 compared with the original 40: 10/40 = 0.25 = 25%.

resolution.takeaway: Percentage points subtract rates; percent change compares their difference with the old rate.

beats.purpose: Consolidate changing bases, composition, reverse percentages, and percentage points.
beats.expectedRealization: Every percent-change calculation begins by identifying its base and direction.
beats.transitionIn: Discounts, increases, reversals, and changing rates all hinge on the same question.

options.text: Identify the amount used as 100% for each change.
Compose successive changes by multiplying their scale factors.
Undo a change by dividing by its scale factor.
Always add successive percentage rates.
Treat percentage points and relative percent change as identical.

response.feedback: Track the current whole and whether the calculation moves forward or backward.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Base, multiplier, and direction control the calculation.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Discard rules that ignore a changed base or merge two different meanings of change.

steps.title: Base
steps.body: Ask what amount counts as 100% at this step.

steps.title: Direction
steps.body: Move forward by multiplying; recover the old value by dividing.

steps.title: Language
steps.body: Use percentage points for direct differences between rates and percent change for change relative to the old rate.

notes: The generated opening establishes a moving reference whole before the approved successive-discount contrast.
